context: A guide's talk for visitors to the Tarnside Steam Railway

cues.t: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer guide talking to visitors at a heritage steam railway. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the Tarnside Steam Railway. My name's Alastair, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you board, I'll give you a bit of background and a few tips for the day.

Visitors often imagine that this line was built to bring holidaymakers up to the lakes. Tourists did use it later on, and local farmers sent some of their produce down on it too. But the reason it was built, back in eighteen sixty-three, was to carry slate from the quarries at the top of the valley down to the coast. When the quarries closed, the line's days were numbered, and the last train ran in nineteen sixty-four.

Reopening it took twenty-two years. We did receive a government grant, but that only paid for repairing one bridge. And some people think the company sold off land along the line, which isn't true. The restoration was really made possible by ordinary members of the public. Thousands of people sent in small donations, often just a few pounds at a time, and that's what paid for most of the work.
The first restored section opened in nineteen eighty-six, and our volunteers have been extending the line a little further ever since.

Now, a couple of things are different this season. Ticket prices are the same as last year, and dogs are still welcome on board, as they've always been. But your ticket is no longer for one journey only. It's now valid all day, so you can get on and off at any station, and ride as many times as you like.

A word about safety. You may get a bit of soot on your clothes, but it brushes off easily, so don't worry about that. And the guard locks the doors before we set off, so you needn't do anything there. What I must ask you not to do is to lean out of the windows. The tunnel at Scar Bank is very narrow, and there's hardly any room on either side of the train.

And here's my top tip. You don't need to buy a guidebook, because there's a free leaflet in every carriage. There's no advantage in catching the first train of the day either, because it's always the busiest. But do try to sit on the left-hand side as we go up the valley, because that's where you'll get the best view of the waterfall.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

Now, if you look at the map in front of you, I'll show you what there is to see at this end of the line. We're standing in the car park, at the south of the site. The railway line runs straight across the map from west to east, and to reach the station, you walk north up the path and cross the line by the footbridge.
Before you get to the bridge, you'll come to the gift shop. As you walk north up the path, it's on your left, just before the steps.

Once you've crossed the footbridge, turn right and follow the fence beside the line. Keep walking east, past the old water tower, and right at the far end, in the north-east corner of the site, you'll find the engine shed. You can watch the locomotives being repaired there.

If you turn left off the bridge instead, you'll walk along the platform and past the station building. When you reach the end of the platform, carry on beside the line, and you'll come to the signal box, standing on its own at the far west of the site.
It was built in eighteen ninety and, on most weekends, one of our signalmen will be happy to show you how the levers work.
The museum is easy to find, because it's directly behind the station building, on its north side. It has a fine collection of old posters and uniforms.

And now something for the children. Go back over the bridge to the south side of the line and turn left, heading east. You'll pass the picnic area first. Keep going beyond it, and over in the far south-east of the site is the miniature railway.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
